problem_data.story:
THE PARADOX PROTOCOL

By Anonymous

The holding facility in Cliffside, Fendria had been constructed with remarkable precision. Patrick Harrison had seen plenty of detention centers during his career in international diplomacy, but nothing quite matched the sterile efficiency of this one. Every surface gleamed under the facility's distinctive emerald lighting—a wavelength the Fendrians had determined optimal for concentration and compliance. The green glow bathed everything, making accurate observation of his surroundings nearly impossible.

The Fendrians, Harrison reflected as he stretched out on the uncomfortably rigid cot, were nothing if not meticulous. All the preliminary intelligence reports had emphasized this trait; their obsession with precision and logical consistency had made them extraordinarily successful in fields like data science and blockchain technology. Within the past decade, they'd revolutionized digital security protocols and were on the verge of creating an unhackable global network. Before long, they'd control the infrastructure of international communications, and then—inevitably—they'd leverage that control into political dominance.

An outcome, the Coalition of Democratic Nations was certain, that would be catastrophic for global freedom.

Harrison sighed and stared at the ceiling. He'd been in isolation for four days now, with nothing to occupy his mind but his own thoughts. He'd tried mental exercises, memory games, even attempting to compose poetry in his head—but his talents didn't lie in creative writing. He couldn't pick the lock with his bare hands; he couldn't even influence the probability that his guards might make a mistake.

He could do, as a matter of fact, precisely nothing except wait. He wished the Fendrians had at least provided him with reading material. A technical manual on water management systems would have been better than this endless boredom.

In any reasonably-run prison, he told himself with frustration, there would at least be other inmates. But in this Fendrian facility, Harrison was completely alone.

True, every evening technicians came and subjected him to intensive language training while he was unconscious, but Harrison got no enjoyment from that. Now he could discuss everything from game theory to entrepreneurship in flawless Fendrian, but he had no one to talk to. He shifted position on the cot and examined the walls again. The Fendrians were thorough; there wasn't even a scratch to distract him.

He wasn't tired and he wasn't hungry; they'd provided him with nutritionally optimized meal replacements. But he was desperately bored and ready to talk to anyone about anything, just for human—or quasi-human—contact.

As he reached this conclusion, the door opened with a pneumatic hiss. Harrison stood quickly and turned to face his visitor.

Under the green illumination, the Fendrian's skin appeared an odd shade—neither quite one color nor another. The being was tall, and Harrison found himself squinting, trying to discern the natural pigmentation beneath the facility's chromatic distortion. The Fendrian's complexion reminded him of deep ocean water under certain lighting conditions. Life throughout the explored regions seemed to favor humanoid forms; Harrison didn't know why, and the scientists back home had offered dozens of theories without reaching consensus. Harrison didn't particularly care; it wasn't his area of expertise.

The Fendrian studied him through pale, almost colorless eyes. "You are Patrick Harrison," he said in a flat, emotionless tone.

It was a ritual, Harrison had learned. "You are Fendrian," he replied.

The being nodded once. "I am Oliver Carter of Fendria," he said. The formalities completed, he entered the cell, the door sliding shut behind him. Harrison briefly considered attacking, but dismissed the idea. He was a prisoner, and it would be foolish to assume his captors lacked hidden defenses beyond the visible neural disruptor holstered at Carter's side and the small blade at his belt.

"What is your purpose here?" Harrison said. The Fendrian language—apparently the entire nation spoke one standardized dialect—was rigid and mathematical in structure, but easily learned under hypnotic conditioning. It was the most ruthlessly logical linguistic construction Harrison had encountered in his diplomatic career, reminiscent of formal logic systems he'd studied years ago.

"I have no purpose here," Carter said, standing near the door. His uniform was the standard Fendrian military issue—a deep forest green that supposedly complemented their natural coloring, though Harrison couldn't verify this under the current lighting. "Do you have additional questions?"

Harrison suppressed a sigh. "Why have you come to this location?" he asked, mentally adjusting to the Fendrian literalist interpretation of language.

"I have been ordered to come to this location," Carter said, "by the Director. The Director requires information from you."

The Fendrian term wasn't quite "requires"—it was more specific, roughly translating to "demands with full legal authority." Harrison filed the distinction away. "Why did the Director not come to me?" he asked.

"The Director is the Director," Carter said, as if this explained everything. "You will go to the Director. This is the command."

Harrison smoothed his hair and straightened his posture. "I acknowledge the Director's command," he said—another required response. Everyone acknowledged the Director's commands in Fendria. Failure to do so meant immediate termination.

But Harrison meant exactly what he'd said. He was going to follow the Director's commands—and in doing so, eliminate the Fendrian threat to global democratic governance forever.

That, after all, was his mission.

---

The Director's office was large, rectangular, and overwhelmingly gray. The walls were dark gray, the furniture—a single imposing desk, several rigid chairs, and a row of filing cabinets—was light gray metal, and even the window treatments were slate-colored. More importantly, Harrison noted with relief, the lighting here was neutral—standard white illumination that allowed accurate color perception for the first time since his arrival.

The Director himself was unlike anything Harrison had expected based on his cell observations. A Fendrian over six and a half feet tall with correspondingly broad shoulders, the Director sat behind his desk, fingers steepled precisely, studying Harrison and his two escorts. In the neutral lighting, Harrison could finally see what the intelligence briefings had described: the distinctive pigmentation that set Fendrians apart from humans. The Director's skin had that characteristic tint—the same shade as the ocean photographs Harrison had seen in geography texts, the color of water under an afternoon sky.

The escorts stood on either side of their prisoner, motionless as statues. Their complexions matched the Director's precisely—that same aquatic hue that seemed to shimmer slightly under direct illumination.

Harrison wasn't trying to escape. He wasn't begging for mercy. He wasn't defying authority. He was simply answering questions.

The Fendrians valued clarity above all else. They were a logical people. The Director had begun with Harrison's nationality, his full name, his biological sex, and whether his appearance was typical for his species.

Harrison was now addressing the last question. "Some humans are taller than I am," he said, "and some are shorter."

"Specify the range," the Director commanded.

Harrison shrugged slightly. "Some exceed two meters in height," he said, using the Fendrian measurement system, "while others are below one meter." He saw no need to mention that both extremes were exceptional cases. "Additionally, there is a category of humans who are typically between forty and sixty centimeters tall—usually around forty-five centimeters. We call these 'children,'" he added helpfully.

"'Typically'?" the Director said sharply. "We require precision here. We are a scientific society. We demand exactitude."

Harrison nodded quickly. "My species is more... variable," he said apologetically.

"Imprecise," the Director muttered. His complexion seemed to darken momentarily with irritation—Harrison noticed the way Fendrian skin shifted toward deeper shades of its base color when emotions ran high.

"Undoubtedly," Harrison agreed politely. "I'll provide the most accurate information I can."

"You will answer my questions," the Director said, "with complete precision." He paused, his expression unchanging. "You arrived in Fendria via aircraft," he continued. "Explain the purpose."

"My assignment required it," Harrison said.

"An obvious falsehood," the Director said. "The aircraft crashed; our analysis proves this conclusively."

"Correct," Harrison said.

"And your assignment is to crash aircraft?" the Director said. "This is inefficient."

Harrison shrugged again. "What I state is accurate," he said. "Do you possess verification methods?"

"We do," the Director told him. "We are a precise and scientific nation. A truth-verification system has been calibrated to your physiology. It will be applied to you now."

Harrison looked toward the door as it opened, admitting two technicians pushing a large device. The machine was painted in the standard Fendrian equipment color—a muted greenish-gray that supposedly reduced visual fatigue during extended operations. It was bulky, angular, and metallic, mounted on wheels, covered with displays, sensors, blinking indicators, cables, and featuring a seat with restraints. It was clearly a polygraph system—and Harrison marveled again at this society. Coalition technology had nothing approaching their mastery of physical sciences; adapting a hypnotic language-training program to an alien mind so rapidly had been impressive enough, but calibrating the extraordinarily sensitive mechanisms of a polygraph to unfamiliar physiology was nearly miraculous.

The Fendrians, under different circumstances, would have been valuable allies in promoting global stability and cultural exchange.

Being what they are, however, they could only threaten the democratic world order. And Harrison's understanding of that threat grew with each passing hour.

He hoped the polygraph had been calibrated correctly. If it indicated deception, he wouldn't survive long, and both his mission and his strong personal preference demanded his continued survival.

He swallowed hard. But when the technicians strapped him into the seat, attached sensors and electrodes to his body at various points, and tightened the final restraints, he offered no resistance.

"We will test the device," the Director said. "In what location are you?"

"In the Director's office," Harrison said calmly.

"Are you standing or seated?"

"I am seated," Harrison said.

"Are you a vrakken?" the Director asked. A vrakken was a small Fendrian animal, Harrison knew, something like an oversized beetle with an iridescent green carapace.

"I am not," he said.

The Director glanced at his technicians for confirmation, then nodded at their signal. "You will now state a falsehood," he said. "Are you standing or seated?"

"I am standing," Harrison said.

The technicians signaled again. The Director looked satisfied. "The device," he announced, "has been successfully calibrated to your physiology. Questioning will now proceed."

Harrison swallowed again. The test seemed inadequate to him. But the Fendrians knew their business better than anyone else could. They had the methodology and the logic and the expertise.

He hoped they were right.

The Director was studying him intently. Harrison tried to appear cooperative. "Why did you come to Fendria?" the Director asked.

"My assignment required it," Harrison said.

The Director nodded. "Your assignment is to crash aircraft," he said. "This is wasteful, but the device indicates truth. Very well; we will learn more about your assignment. Was the crash deliberate?"

Harrison maintained a neutral expression. "Yes," he said.

The Director's eyes narrowed slightly. "Very well," he said. "Was your assignment completed when the aircraft crashed?"

"No," Harrison said.

"What additional objectives does your assignment include?" the Director asked.

Harrison decided to introduce his first complication. "Remaining alive."

The Director's face flushed with agitation, the pigmentation intensifying to a shade that reminded Harrison of photographs he'd seen of the deep sea—that particular color water took on far below the surface, where sunlight barely penetrated. "Do not waste time with self-evident facts!" he said sharply. "Do not attempt to deceive us; we are a logical and scientific people! Answer appropriately."

"I have stated the truth," Harrison said.

"But it is not—not the truth we seek," the Director said.

Harrison shrugged. "I responded to your question," he said. "I was unaware that truth had multiple categories. Surely truth is truth, just as the Director is the Director?"

"I—" The Director stopped himself. "You attempt to confuse the Director," he said finally, his voice controlled again, his complexion gradually returning to its normal shade. "But the Director will not be confused. We have specialists in logical analysis who will advise the Director. They will be summoned."

Harrison's escorts had been standing idle now that their prisoner was restrained in the polygraph. The Director gestured and they exited quickly.

The Director looked down at Harrison. "You will discover that you cannot deceive us," he said. "You will discover that such primitive attempts will achieve nothing."

Harrison sincerely hoped so.

---

The logic specialists arrived within minutes, and Harrison was firmly informed that logical paradoxes would not confuse anyone in Fendria. Russell's paradox, the liar's paradox, Zeno's paradoxes, and all the other classic logical puzzles were elementary material for the Fendrians. "They can be resolved through formal logic systems," one specialist, a slight being named Jordan West, told Harrison coolly. West's skin matched the others precisely—that same distinctive color that Harrison had noted throughout the population. "Naturally, you would not comprehend the formal systems. But that is irrelevant. You need only understand that we cannot be confused by such methods."

"Excellent," Harrison said.

The specialist blinked. "Excellent?" he said.

"Naturally," Harrison said pleasantly.

The specialist's expression hardened, his jaw tightening, his complexion shifting to a deeper, more intense shade of its base color—like bruised sky, Harrison thought, or twilight reflected on still water. "Your strategy has failed," the specialist said, "yet you call this excellent. You can only mean that your strategy differs from what we have assumed."

"Correct," Harrison said.

There was a brief silence. The specialist's expression shifted to something like satisfaction, his skin gradually lightening again. He examined the polygraph displays carefully. "What is your strategy?" he asked quietly.

"To answer your questions truthfully and logically," Harrison said.

The silence lasted longer this time.

"The device indicates truth," the specialist said finally, his tone suggesting awe. "Therefore, you must be betraying your own nation. You must want us to dominate your region, and have come here secretly to assist us."

Harrison was grateful that wasn't a question. It was, after all, the only logical conclusion.

But it happened to be wrong.

---

"Your nation is called the Bristol Region?" the Director asked. Several minutes had passed; the specialists were clustered around the desk, their identical coloring creating an almost uniform visual effect—like a row of identical figures, distinguished only by height and build. Harrison remained strapped to the polygraph; a logical society might use a traitor, but a logical society does not trust him.

"Sometimes," Harrison said.

"It has other names?" the Director asked.

"It has no name," Harrison said truthfully. The Fendrian idiom was similar to English; certainly a nation had no name of its own. People assigned names to it, that was all. It possessed none inherently.

"Yet you call it the Bristol Region?" the Director said.

"I do," Harrison said, "for convenience in communication."

"Do you know its precise geographical coordinates?" the Director asked.

"Not with exactitude," Harrison said.

There was a stir among the specialists. "But you can locate it again," the Director said.

"I can," Harrison said.

"And you will provide us with information about it?" the Director continued.

"I will," Harrison said, "to the extent of my knowledge."

"We will require information about defensive capabilities," the Director said, "and about strategic planning and fortifications. But we must first understand the decision-making structure in your region. Is your nation affiliated with others in a governmental alliance, or does it exist independently?"

Harrison almost smiled. "Both," he said.

A brief silence was broken by one of the specialists. "We have theorized that a subordinate entity may be permitted to make certain decisions independently, with only major decisions reserved for the central authority. This seems inefficient and error-prone, yet it is a possible system. Is this what you mean?"

Very astute, Harrison thought. "It is," he said.

"Then the government that controls multiple nations is supreme," the Director said.

"It is," Harrison said.

"Who exercises this control?" the Director asked.

The crucial question had finally been asked. Harrison was grateful that the logical Fendrians had chosen to begin systematically, rather than jumping to questions about military capabilities first; it saved considerable time.

"The answer to that question," Harrison said, "cannot be provided to you."

"Every factual question has an answer," the Director said sharply. "No paradox is involved here; a government exists, and some entity governs. Perhaps multiple entities share this function; perhaps automated systems perform the work. But where there is government, there is a governor. Is this not so?"

"Certainly," Harrison said. "It is completely obvious and accurate."

"The nation from which you come is part of an alliance of nations that are governed, you have stated," the Director continued.

"Correct," Harrison said.

"Then there is a governor for this alliance," the Director said.

"Correct," Harrison said again.

The Director exhaled slowly. "Describe this governor to us," he said.

Harrison shrugged. "The description cannot be provided to you."

The Director turned to his specialists and a brief whispered consultation occurred. When it ended, the Director returned his attention to Harrison. "Is the limitation in you?" he asked. "Are you somehow unable to describe this government?"

"It can be described," Harrison said.

"Then you will suffer negative consequences if you describe it to us?" the Director continued.

"I will not," Harrison said.

This prompted another consultation. With some satisfaction, Harrison noticed that the Fendrians were becoming visibly uncertain; their skin tones were fluctuating subtly, shifting between lighter and deeper variations of that characteristic color as emotions waxed and waned.

The plan was working.

The Director had finished conferring. "You are attempting again to confuse us," he said.

Harrison shook his head earnestly. "I am attempting," he said, "not to confuse you."

"Then I demand an answer," the Director said.

"I request that I be permitted to ask a question," Harrison said.

The Director hesitated, then nodded once. "Ask it," he said. "We will answer if we determine it appropriate."

Harrison tried to look grateful. "Very well," he said. "What is your system of government?"

The Director gestured to a heavy-set being, who stepped forward from the group of Fendrians, inclined his head toward Harrison, and began speaking in a surprisingly melodious voice. "Our government is the only logical form of government," he said. "The Director commands all, and citizens obey. Through this method, uniformity is achieved, and this uniformity enables rapid action and concentrated force. All Fendrians act simultaneously in the same manner. The Director is selected by the previous Director; through this method we ensure consistent wisdom and stable judgment."

"You have heard our government described," the Director said. "Now, you will describe yours to us."

Harrison shook his head. "If you insist," he said, "I'll attempt it. But you will not understand it."

The Director's expression hardened. "We will understand," he said. "Begin. Who governs you?"

"No one," Harrison said.

"But you are governed?"

Harrison nodded. "Yes."

"Then there is a governor," the Director insisted.

"Correct," Harrison said. "But everyone is the governor."

"Then there is no government," the Director said. "There is no unified decision-making."

"No," Harrison said calmly, "there are many decisions binding on all citizens."

"Who makes them binding?" the Director asked. "Who compels you to accept these decisions? Some of them must be unfavorable to some individuals?"

"Many of them are unfavorable," Harrison said. "But we are not compelled to accept them."

"Do you act against your own interests?"

Harrison shrugged. "Not knowingly," he said. The Director glanced sharply at the technicians monitoring the polygraph. Harrison turned to observe their expressions—their faces all bore that same distinctive hue, unchanged by emotional response as they focused on their instruments. They needed no words; the polygraph was clearly indicating that he was telling the truth. But the truth wasn't making any sense. "I warned you that you wouldn't understand it," he said.

"It is a flaw in your description," the Director said, his voice strained, his complexion darkening to what Harrison now recognized as the Fendrian indicator of extreme frustration.

"My description is as precise as possible," Harrison said.

The Director breathed heavily. "Let us try a different approach," he said. "Everyone is the governor. Do you share a collective consciousness? A hive mind has been theorized, though we have encountered no examples—"

"Neither have we," Harrison said. "We are all individuals, like yourselves."

"But with no single director to formulate policy, to make decisions—"

"We have no need of one," Harrison said calmly.

"Ah," the Director said suddenly, as if seeing clarity ahead. "And why not?"

"We call our form of government 'democracy,'" Harrison said. "It means government by the people. There is no need for another director."

One of the specialists spoke up suddenly. "The individuals themselves govern each other?" he said. "This is clearly impossible; no single individual can possess the force to compel acceptance of commands. Without this force, there can be no effective government."

"That is our form of government," Harrison said.

"You are lying," the specialist said.

One of the technicians interjected: "The device indicates—"

"Then the device is malfunctioning," the specialist said. "It will be recalibrated."

Harrison wondered, as the technicians began arguing, how long they'd spend examining the polygraph before they realized it had no malfunction to correct. He hoped it wouldn't take too long; he could foresee another period of tedious boredom ahead. And besides, he was getting homesick for the Bristol Region.

---

It took five days—but boredom never really materialized. Harrison found himself receiving more attention than he'd anticipated; one by one, the specialists visited his cell, each with a different approach to resolving the apparent contradictions in his statements. Under the facility's green lighting, they all looked somewhat different than they had in the Director's office—the chromatic distortion making their features seem almost alien, their skin taking on an unusual cast that made Harrison's initial observations seem questionable.

Some left angry. Others simply left, bewildered.

On the fifth day, Harrison escaped.

It wasn't particularly difficult; he hadn't expected it to be. Even the most logical of thinking beings possesses a subconscious mind as well as a conscious one, and one method of dealing with an insoluble problem is to make the problem vanish. There were only two ways to accomplish that, and eliminating the problem's focal point was somewhat more complicated. That couldn't be done by the subconscious mind alone; the conscious mind had to participate. And it couldn't.

Because that would require recognizing, fully and consciously, that the problem was genuinely insoluble. And the Fendrians weren't capable of that kind of thinking.

Harrison was grateful that their genius had been confined to the physical and computational sciences. Any insight into psychology would have given them the key to his existence and his entire strategy within seconds.

But then, it was precisely that lack of insight that had necessitated this particular mission. That, and the authoritarian political structure of Fendria.

The same lack of insight allowed the Fendrian subconscious to work on his escape without any troublesome interference from deep reflection. Someone left a door unlocked and a weapon accessible—all quite unintentional, Harrison was certain. Reaching his aircraft was slightly more complicated, but presented no fundamental obstacles; he was airborne, and then beyond Fendrian airspace, within a few hours of leaving the cell.

He set his course, relaxed, and cleared his mind. He had no telepathic abilities, but the specialists at Coalition Intelligence did; he couldn't receive messages, but he could send them. He sent one now.

*Mission accomplished; the Fendrians won't be expanding their authoritarian model into neighboring regions anytime soon. They've been given a conceptual puzzle—a beautifully indigestible puzzle that will occupy them until they finally manage to comprehend it. But they can't comprehend it and remain what they are; you need to embrace democratic principles, to some degree, to understand the concept. What makes us obey laws we ourselves create? What makes us obey laws that disadvantage us personally? Enlightened self-interest, naturally—but try to make a Fendrian grasp it!*

*With one director and one standardized language, they simply weren't equipped for this kind of translation. They were too successful with physical sciences to pursue psychology or political science seriously. No social sciences, no insight into my mind or their own—and that means no translation.*

*But—damn it—I wish I were home already. I'm absolutely bored out of my mind!*

---

Back in Lincoln, Nordavia, at Coalition Intelligence headquarters, Director Giovanni Potter received Harrison's mental transmission and smiled. The Fendrian problem had been neutralized, at least for the foreseeable future. They'd spend years, perhaps decades, trying to understand how a government could function without a single director, how laws could be binding without a single enforcer, how order could emerge from apparent chaos.

And by the time they figured it out—if they ever did—they'd no longer be the threat they currently posed. Understanding democracy required experiencing it, and experiencing it would change them fundamentally.

Potter drafted a brief report for the Coalition Council, noting the successful completion of the mission. Patrick Harrison, specialist in strategic planning and international diplomacy, had once again proven himself invaluable.

The report concluded: "The Paradox Protocol remains our most effective non-violent method for neutralizing authoritarian expansionist threats. Recommend continued deployment in similar situations."

Potter signed the report and filed it securely. Then he sent a message to Harrison: *Welcome home when you arrive. Well done.*

Harrison, still hours away from home, received the message as a vague sense of approval and warmth. It wasn't much, but it helped with the boredom.

He wondered what his next assignment would be. Probably something in Rosewood, Nordavia, where a new separatist movement was gaining strength. Or perhaps Cliffside again, if the Fendrians recovered faster than expected.

Either way, he'd be ready. That was his job, after all—to preserve the democratic way of life, one paradox at a time.
